title: Many Judaisms
hook: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argue over law and Temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Yannai wore two crowns, and a sage told him one should be enough. Your line was heroes can change. Today, the arguments in Jerusalem multiply.

One man in Jerusalem wants to find the right way to live, so he tries all of them. That's how the historian Josephus describes his youth. There were, he says, three schools of thought among the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes. He went through all three, from the inside. Then, still not satisfied, he went out to the desert to live with a teacher named Bannus, who wore clothes made from what grew on trees, ate only what grew wild, and bathed in cold water day and night. Only after that did he come back to the city and choose. In those days, being Jewish came in more than one shape.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN TRIES ALL THREE.` → `A TEACHER IN THE DESERT.` → `MORE THAN ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Josephus lays out the schools. The Pharisees keep many customs handed down from the fathers that aren't written in the law of Moses, and teach that souls live on after death. The Sadducees hold that only the written laws are binding, and say the soul does not outlive the body; Josephus says they were fewer but included people of high rank. The Essenes live in close communities and share their property, so that no one among them is rich and no one is poor. And Josephus adds a fourth group, followers of Judas the Galilean, who say God alone is their ruler and will call no man master. The Mishnah lets us hear two of these groups argue. In tractate Yadayim, the Sadducees complain to the Pharisees: you say holy scriptures make the hands impure, but the books the Mishnah calls Hamiram don't? Some readers take that word to mean Homer. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai answers, and the debate goes on, round after round. Notice the shape. These aren't people who've lost their faith. They care so much about the Torah and the Temple that they argue about every detail: what counts as Torah, who should run the Temple, what happens after death, how to live. There were many ways to be Jewish, and the Mishnah keeps the Sadducees' complaint in their own words.
screen: `PHARISEES: CUSTOMS FROM THE FATHERS.` · `SADDUCEES: ONLY WHAT'S WRITTEN.` · `ESSENES: EVERYTHING SHARED.` · then, large: `SADDUCEES AND PHARISEES ARGUE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a group whose way differs from yours, another congregation, another party, a family down the street that keeps its customs differently or keeps none, and picture one actual person from it, with a face and a name. Ask what they care about enough to argue for, and find one thing you can honestly respect, without having to agree. If you pray, use words from your tradition to wish them well.
Many Judaisms. Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others, all arguing over Torah and Temple in the same land at the same time. Today's word.
Your line: many ways then too. They argued because they cared so much. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews today belong to different movements and communities, such as Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others, and study the Second Temple sects through the Mishnah, the Talmud and the writings of Josephus.

chat.says: Back in Josephus's day, did all Jews agree on how to practice their faith?
options: No: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argued, all caring deeply about Torah.
Yes, everyone followed the Temple priests, so there were no real disagreements.
No, but only the Pharisees cared about Torah; the rest had given up on it.
chat.meaning: Josephus describes Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and a fourth group, and the Mishnah records Sadducees and Pharisees arguing: many ways, all caring about Torah.

Josephus.meaning: a Jewish historian who tried all three schools as a young man

Pharisees.meaning: a school that kept customs handed down from the fathers

Sadducees.meaning: a school that held only the written laws binding

Essenes.meaning: a school living in close communities, sharing property

Bannus.meaning: a desert teacher Josephus lived with

notes: Josephus paraphrased throughout (Whiston is not on the public-domain list here). Life 2 gives his age (sixteen) and three years with Bannus; the script omits the numbers. Please confirm the Bannus details (clothing from trees, wild food, cold bathing day and night).

Josephus on the Pharisees' unwritten customs is Antiquities 13.10.6; on the soul, Antiquities 18.1.3–4 and War 2.8.14; Sadducees 'few but of high rank' Antiquities 18.1.4; Essenes' common property War 2.8.3; the fourth philosophy Antiquities 18.1.6. Please confirm the summaries are fair to each group.
Mishnah Yadayim 4:6: the Sadducees' complaint about scriptures and 'the books of Homer' and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's reply. Please confirm.

Final teach lines ('There are many ways now too. The arguing itself is a family tradition.') are the writer's framing; Keeper please check tone. howItsDone lists movements without ranking them; please confirm the list.
